annotation.reasoning_summary: The dataset maps individual residential building blocks ('woonblokken') represented as polygons. Although these blocks have aggregated statistics, the features themselves are identifiable real-world residential complexes (managed assets). They are not administrative reporting units (LatticeDS) or exhaustive land-use coverage (CoverageDS), so they fall under ObjectDS.
The dataset maps specific archaeological finds (objects) and locations (cesspits) as points. These are discrete, identifiable real-world entities.
The dataset maps specific archaeological find locations (points) where objects were discovered. Each point represents a distinct, real-world site or object discovery, fitting the ObjectDS criteria.

The layer represents archaeological sites, which are discrete, identifiable, and named real-world objects. Each polygon refers to a specific, historical excavation site (e.g., a specific building's foundation or historical harborfront). Because these are distinct, managed entities with specific location data rather than arbitrary policy zones, ObjectDS is the correct classification.

The map displays specific areas (polygons) where barbecue regulations (rules, restrictions, prohibitions) apply, rather than the parks themselves as the primary entities. This aligns with the PatchDS classification for policy/restriction zones.

The dataset identifies areas with a 'protected' status (stads- en dorpsgezichten). These are defined administrative zones where a specific regulatory policy and conservation status apply, rather than being discrete objects, reporting units, or full-area land-use classifications. As they are selected bounded zones of regulatory applicability, they fit the PatchDS category best.

The map displays point locations where biological surveys (wild bee observations) were conducted. Each point represents a distinct survey site (location/facility) rather than a continuous measurement or an event occurring in time, making ObjectDS the most appropriate classification.

The map displays point locations of honey bee hives (bijenkasten). Each point represents a distinct, identifiable facility or managed location. Although numeric attributes for the number of hives exist, they are attributes of the object rather than the main phenomenon (like a density map). Therefore, it is classified as ObjectDS.

The dataset partitions the city of Amsterdam into zones (soil quality zones) with categorical classifications for soil function and quality (Toplaag, Diepe_laag). As this represents a full-area thematic coverage of soil quality classes, it is classified as CoverageDS and VectorTessellation.

The dataset maps individual trees as point features. Each point represents a distinct, identifiable managed asset/object with specific attributes (species, height, planting year), fulfilling the criteria for ObjectDS.
